# A platform's @run runs before the loop, with the command line; `run` presents
# the window and runs the loop, so the code after it waits for the loop to end.
# Not called, the handler returns, the loop runs with no window, and the timer
# still ticks -- which is how a status bar launched by i3 starts without a
# window. Each run ends from the tick, so "after" appears only where run was
# not called.
#
# testdata/platform_run_handler.txtar is the code.

[!headless] skip 'needs the headless compositor go tool verify provides'

[gtk4] sngl build --lang go --platform gtk4 -o gtk4 app.sngl
[gtk4] exec ./gtk4/app
[gtk4] cmp stdout hidden.txt
[gtk4] exec ./gtk4/app --window x
[gtk4] cmp stdout shown.txt

sngl build --lang go --platform fyne -o fyne app.sngl
exec ./fyne/app
cmp stdout hidden.txt
exec ./fyne/app --window x
cmp stdout shown.txt

-- hidden.txt --
before 0
after
tick 0
-- shown.txt --
before 2
tick 2
-- app.sngl --
import go "sngl:language/go"
import time "sngl:time"
import ui "sngl:ui"

#[go.native("fmt", "fmt.Print")]
func print(s string)

#[go.native("os", "os.Exit")]
func exit(code int)

var n = 0

output {
    go {
        gtk4(@run(args, run) {
            start(args, run)
        })
        fyne(@run(args, run) {
            start(args, run)
        })
    }
}

// Before `run` is before the loop; after it, after the loop has exited. A
// write here is state the tree is built from, not an update to one.
func start(args list<string>, run func()) {
    print("before {args.length}\n")
    n = args.length
    if args.contains("--window") {
        run()
    }
    print("after\n")
}

time.timer(interval=100ms, @tick {
    print("tick {n}\n")
    exit(0)
})

ui.window {
    ui.text(value="{n}")
}
